title: Sleep is the first thing I cut.
dek: Sleeping 6 hours instead of 8 for two weeks buys you 28 extra hours awake. In one study, that much sleep left people as impaired as up to two nights without any, and they barely noticed.
whyThisIdea: Este următoarea idee nefolosită din backlog (#19; am sărit din nou peste #1, #7 și #14, încă marcate ca prea apropiate de articole publicate). Se leagă de „Free time is not free”: aceleași ore, dar întrebarea e în ce stare ești când le folosești, cu studiul Van Dongen (2003) și aritmetica 2 ore × 14 nopți.

entry.title: Sleep is the first thing I cut.
entry.titleHtml: Sleep is the first thing I cut.
entry.dek: Sleeping 6 hours instead of 8 for two weeks buys you 28 extra hours awake. In one study, that much sleep left people as impaired as up to two nights without any, and they barely noticed.
body: “The hour you take from the night, you pay back the next day - with interest.”

Have you ever asked yourself what is the first thing you give up when the week gets full? Today is Saturday, the 14th of November, the middle of the semester, and if you are a student like me, you know exactly how a full week looks. The homework, the lectures, the friends and the phone do not move. There is only one thing in the day that bends without complaining, and it is the night. So the question is: why is sleep always the first thing we cut, when it might be the cheapest thing we have that actually makes us better? Let’s start from the beginning.

The thing I want to look at is sleep, and I did not meet it in a book. I met it at one in the morning, with a deadline and a cold cup of tea. The logic in my head was always very simple: I need more hours, the night has hours, so I take them from the night. Nobody is waiting for my sleep, nobody grades it, nobody sends an email when I skip it. And that, I think now, is exactly the problem.

Firstly, let’s split the idea in two, the way I like to do. “Cheapest upgrade” and “first thing cut”. An upgrade is a word from tech - you buy more memory or a faster processor, and the same machine does more. Sleep costs nothing (no subscription, no app, no equipment) and still it is the thing that decides how well the machine runs the next day. The second half, “first thing cut”, is about why we give it up so easily. Every other thing in the day has someone on the other side - a teacher, a boss, a friend. Sleep has only you, and the cost arrives tomorrow, to a person who is not in the room yet. <u>We cut sleep first not because it is the least important, but because it is the only thing that does not complain.</u>

Secondly, let’s look at a study that measured exactly this, because “sleep is important” is a sentence everybody agrees with and nobody acts on. In 2003, Hans Van Dongen, David Dinges and their colleagues published a paper in the journal Sleep with a title that sounds like accounting: “The Cumulative Cost of Additional Wakefulness”. They took 48 healthy adults, aged 21 to 38, and for 14 days in a row they let them sleep 8, 6 or 4 hours a night. A fourth group was not allowed to sleep at all for 3 days. Every day they tested their attention, their memory and how fast they reacted.

The conclusion of the paper: cutting sleep to 6 hours or less a night produced cognitive deficits equivalent to up to 2 nights of total sleep deprivation. Now let’s do the arithmetic of the “smart move” from the beginning. Sleeping 6 hours instead of 8, for two weeks:
2 hours × 14 nights = 28 extra hours awake
More than a full day. But those 28 hours are spent by a slower version of you - in the worst case, as slow as someone who did not sleep for two nights in a row. You do not win 28 hours. You borrow them, and the interest is paid by every hour you are awake.

And the detail that scared me the most is not the number. The people who slept less were largely unaware of how much worse they were getting. Their feeling of sleepiness went up in the first days and then barely grew, while their performance kept going down. So the one tool you would use to check if you are fine - “I feel fine” - is exactly the tool that stops working first. This is why cutting sleep feels free. The bill is real, you just lose the ability to read it.

Let’s put it a little bit in perspective with a whole year. If 6 hours becomes my normal instead of 8:
2 hours × 365 nights = 730 hours a year
730 ÷ 16 waking hours = about 46 waking days
Forty-six days. In my article about free time, I wrote that free time is not free, because it is the thing you are actually investing. Here they are, a month and a half of them, and the question is not whether I get them, it is what condition I am in when I spend them. If all 730 hours come with a slower head, I am not sure they are worth more than the sleep they replaced.

Thirdly, and this is the counter-case I have to be fair to. Not every short night is a mistake. There are nights when finishing the thing really is more important, like the night before a deadline you cannot move, and one night is not the same as fourteen. People are also different - the study shows groups, not individuals, and a few people really do need less sleep, even if most of us like to believe we are one of them. And the study itself is smaller than its fame: 48 people, in a laboratory, for two weeks. “Up to” is also doing some work in that sentence, because the worst comparison is not the average one. So I read it not as a law, but as a warning that the cost is real, bigger than it feels, and that it adds up.

So here is what I am going to do, because an article like this is worthless if it ends only in agreement. For the next week, I will write down two things every morning: the time I went to bed and the time I woke up. No app, just a line in a notebook. And I will keep one rule: after midnight, no new work starts. If something is not done by then, it gets done tomorrow, by a person who slept. At the end of the week I will add up the hours and see how far from 8 I really am.

For today, that will be all. My personal opinion? I really believe sleep is the most underrated upgrade a student has, and that most of us cut it because it is the only thing that cannot argue back. But I have to be honest about two things. The evidence I used is one famous study in a lab, not my life, and I do not know how much sleep I actually need - nobody can tell me that number except my own notebook. And there is a trap on the other side too: turning sleep into one more thing to optimise, with trackers and scores, can make you worry about it so much that it gets worse. What I take from it is smaller: when the day is too full, cut something that can complain.
In the end, I hope you enjoyed this article and I will leave you with the line that started all of this. Peace!
“The hour you take from the night, you pay back the next day - with interest.”
